overview.intro: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned to India in 1915 and within seven years had transformed Indian politics by demonstrating that a mass movement disciplined by non-violence could be conducted against the strongest administration in the world. This unit covers the early experiments at Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad, the Rowlatt Act agitation, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919 and its consequences, and the first all-India movement of non-cooperation combined with the Khilafat agitation, ending with its suspension after Chauri Chaura in 1922.

blocks.text: Gandhi’s method was established in three local campaigns before he took on a national issue. In Champaran in 1917 he investigated the tinkathia system, by which indigo cultivators were compelled to grow the crop on a fixed share of their land, and though the government tried to prevent his enquiries he persisted, gathered evidence from cultivators, and obtained the appointment of a committee whose findings led to the abolition of the system. In Kheda in 1918, where a poor harvest led peasants to ask for the remission of revenue, Gandhi advised them to withhold payment until the demand was reassessed, and the administration conceded partial remission while refusing to make it a precedent.

blocks.text: In each case the pattern was the same: he began by establishing the facts, he used non-violent non-cooperation rather than confrontation, he accepted a limited victory rather than overreaching, and he built the confidence of the participants. These campaigns demonstrated to the wider political class that satyagraha could work against the administration without producing a violent clash.

learn.title: The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh

blocks.text: The Rowlatt Act of 1919, passed on the recommendation of a committee chaired by Justice Rowlatt, allowed detention without trial and trial without jury for offences described as sedition, on the argument that wartime emergency measures should continue. Gandhi called it a blow struck at civil liberty and called for a nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919, with fasting, prayer and suspension of business as forms of protest. The response was widespread, and in several towns processions led to clashes with the police, which led to arrests including that of Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satya Pal in Amritsar.

On 13 April 1919 a large crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh, some to protest the arrests and some to attend the Baisakhi festival, in an enclosed ground with narrow exits. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered his troops to fire on the crowd without warning, continuing until the ammunition was nearly exhausted, and the official figure of 379 dead was widely regarded as an undercount with over 1,200 wounded. Dyer was subsequently removed from his post but received a public subscription in his honour in Britain, and the Hunter Committee of inquiry criticised his action while the House of Lords praised it. The massacre destroyed what remained of trust in the benevolence of British rule and convinced many nationalists, including Rabindranath Tagore, who renounced his knighthood, that the moral case for the connection had collapsed.

blocks.text: The non-cooperation resolution was adopted at the Calcutta special session of September 1920 and confirmed at Nagpur in December, in combination with the Khilafat movement led by the Ali brothers over the terms imposed on the Ottoman caliph after the First World War. Gandhi argued that the two could be united in a single movement for swaraj. The programme called for the surrender of titles and honours, the boycott of schools, colleges, courts and councils, the boycott of foreign cloth, and the adoption of khadi and Indian institutions in their place.

The movement reached further into Indian society than anything before it. Students left government schools, lawyers abandoned the courts, the councils were boycotted so completely that the first elections under the 1919 constitution saw a very low turnout, and the bonfires of foreign cloth became the period’s defining image. Communal harmony was a stated aim, with Hindus and Muslims appearing together at demonstrations, and the Nagpur session made the Congress a membership-based organisation with a constitution capable of mass work.

blocks.caption: The non-cooperation programme
rows: Arbitration by panchayats and Indian lawyers in national causes

learn.title: Chauri Chaura and the suspension of 1922

blocks.text: On 5 February 1922 at Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur district, a crowd of demonstrators clashed with the police, the police station was set on fire and twenty-two policemen who were inside died. Gandhi, who had warned that the movement was running ahead of its non-violent discipline, decided that the country had not yet learnt non-violence, and he suspended the movement with immediate effect. He was widely criticised for the decision, including by Motilal Nehru and C.R. Das, who argued that a movement should not be abandoned on the failure of a small minority, but he held to the principle that the method mattered as much as the objective.

The suspension ended the first phase of mass politics but left a durable legacy: the Congress had become a mass organisation, khadi and national education had a permanent place in nationalist life, and the technique of non-violent non-cooperation had been demonstrated on a national scale. The following decade, the Simon Commission, the Nehru Report and finally the Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930 built on that base.

questions.explanation: Khadi embodied both economic self-sufficiency and the refusal of mill-made foreign cloth.

questions.prompt: State four features of the non-cooperation programme.
questions.answer: Four features are: the surrender of titles and honours conferred by the government; the boycott of government schools and colleges in favour of national institutions; the boycott of law courts and legislative councils; and the refusal of foreign cloth in favour of khadi and Indian manufacture. The use of Indian languages in national schools is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each feature needs the alternative that replaced it, since non-cooperation was a substitution and not only a refusal.

questions.prompt: Explain why Gandhi suspended the non-cooperation movement in 1922.
questions.answer: At Chauri Chaura on 5 February 1922 a crowd set fire to a police station and twenty-two policemen died, which was a clear departure from the non-violence on which the movement was founded. Gandhi held that the means and the ends were inseparable, so a movement for swaraj could not be conducted through violence without defeating its own purpose. He also judged that the country as a whole had not yet been disciplined in non-violence, and that continuing would have encouraged further outbreaks rather than building the moral force he regarded as essential. He therefore suspended the movement with immediate effect, accepting severe criticism from within the Congress, including from Motilal Nehru and C.R. Das, who argued that the actions of a minority should not halt a mass movement. The decision established that method was a condition of the struggle and not a matter of tactics.
questions.explanation: The answer needs the principle and the practical judgement, not just the event that triggered it.

questions.prompt: Describe the events of 1919 in India and assess their consequences.
questions.answer: The year opened with the passing of the Rowlatt Act, which continued wartime powers of detention without trial and trial without jury and was described by Gandhi as a blow at civil liberty. He called a hartal for 6 April 1919 with fasting and the suspension of business, and while much of the country observed it peacefully, clashes in several towns led to arrests, including those of Dr Kitchlew and Dr Satya Pal in Amritsar. Crowd gatherings followed in protest, and on 13 April 1919 at Jallianwala Bagh, an enclosed ground with narrow exits, Brigadier-General Dyer ordered his troops to fire on the gathering without warning until ammunition was nearly exhausted, killing hundreds and wounding many more. The consequences were profound. The Hunter Committee criticised Dyer while the House of Lords praised him, which showed how divided British opinion was. Tagore renounced his knighthood. The moral claim of British rule was destroyed for a very large number of Indians, moderate as well as extremist, and it was this that made the adoption of non-cooperation the following year possible, with the Congress deciding that cooperation could no longer be offered to such a government.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the sequence of the year and a reasoned assessment of the political consequences rather than only a description of the massacre.

questions.prompt: Gandhi described non-cooperation as a settled policy rather than an expedient. Using the programme of 1920–22, explain what he meant.
questions.answer: He meant that non-cooperation was not a tactic to be abandoned when results were slow but a principle about how power actually worked. The programme rested on the argument that the colonial government existed because Indians cooperated with it at every level, so the withdrawal of that cooperation would remove its foundation rather than attack it physically. Each item followed from that logic: titles and honours lent legitimacy and were surrendered; schools and colleges reproduced the administration’s values and were replaced by national institutions; courts gave the dispute an authority the rulers controlled and were replaced by arbitration; councils gave the rule a constitutional fig leaf and were boycotted until swaraj was granted; and foreign cloth financed the deindustrialisation of India, so it was refused in favour of khadi. Because the policy depended on moral pressure rather than force, its discipline was not optional, and that is exactly why Gandhi treated the violence at Chauri Chaura as a failure of the policy itself and not as an isolated incident to be ignored. The consistency between withdrawing over one incident and pressing on for years over an injustice is what marks a settled policy rather than an expedient.
questions.explanation: The answer earns marks for showing the underlying theory of power, mapping each programme item to it, and explaining the discipline as a consequence of the same theory.
